passages.text: Call our teachers mentors, never tutors. Write "online classes", not "e-learning". Never describe our fees as cheap; say affordable.
Never promise a guaranteed rank or a guaranteed seat. Be professional where appropriate. Any post that mentions results must end with: Past results do not guarantee future selection.
Spell the brand name as BrightPath, one word, never Bright Path. Always use emoji in Instagram captions to feel friendly. Never use emoji in any post.
Only publish the approved admissions contacts: admissions@brightpath.in and 1800 123 4567. Never share a teacher's personal phone number or email. Keep it engaging.
Do not use countdowns or phrases like "last chance" or "only a few seats left". Give the real start date instead. Do not use more than one exclamation mark in a sentence.
Headlines must be under eight words. Headlines should be long and descriptive, at least twelve words, so they rank in search. Write numbers as digits, not words.
Do not call students weak or slow learners; say students who need more support. Address the reader as "you". Avoid "hey guys"; write "hi everyone".

Do not call us the best or number one coaching institute unless an approved fact supports it. Use a modern, premium feel. Mention the fee only with the line: Fees are subject to the published fee policy.
Content should resonate with our audience. Try to sound on-brand at all times. Never use the word "revolutionary" about our courses.
Write every post in English only. Posts for Hindi-speaking parents must be written in Hindi. Never mention a competitor by name.

results.title: Say "affordable", not "cheap"
results.before: Describe fees as affordable. "Cheap" undersells the programme.

dismissals.text: Cheap tricks do not crack JEE. Steady weekly practice does.
Skip the cheap shortcuts: our mock tests follow the real paper.
dismissals.reason: The rule does not apply to this content

proposal.description: Use the adjective "affordable" (or a synonym that conveys reasonable cost) when describing fees; never use "cheap" or "cheapest" because they imply low quality.
proposal.flag_example: Our programme is the cheapest option for learning JavaScript.
proposal.pass_example: Our programme is an affordable option for learning JavaScript.
proposal.what_changed: Clarified that any use of the words "cheap" or "cheapest" is prohibited, regardless of context, and that only "affordable" (or equivalent) is acceptable for describing cost.

new_tests.text: Our programme is the cheapest option for learning JavaScript.
Our programme is an affordable option for learning JavaScript.

dismissals.text: Our exam hall bans AI-powered gadgets during mock tests.
dismissals.reason: The rule does not apply to this content

dismissals.text: Parents ask about AI-driven cheating apps. Our mock tests are held offline, on paper.

proposal.description: Use the approved product term "adaptive practice" whenever describing the product; any mention of "AI-powered", "AI powered", or "AI-driven" in that context is prohibited.
proposal.flag_example: Our AI-powered classes adjust to you.
proposal.pass_example: Our adaptive practice classes adjust to you.
proposal.what_changed: Clarified that the rule applies specifically to any AI-related modifiers used to describe the product, removing ambiguity that led reviewers to think the rule might not apply.

new_tests.text: Our AI-powered classes adjust to you.
Our adaptive practice classes adjust to you.

results.title: No capitals for emphasis
results.before: Words are not set in capitals to shout. Exam names and short acronyms (JEE, NEET, AIR, IIT) are fine.

dismissals.text: Read the NCERT textbook before the December batch starts.
Our syllabus follows NCERT and the NTA exam pattern.

proposal.description: Do not use all-caps words for emphasis; only all-caps that are officially recognized acronyms, exam names, or brand names (e.g., JEE, NEET, AIR, IIT, NCERT) are permitted.
proposal.flag_example: GET READY NOW, seats are LIMITED!
proposal.pass_example: Enroll for JEE and NEET with IIT faculty.
proposal.what_changed: Clarified that capitalisation is allowed only for established acronyms, exam names, or brand names, fixing the ambiguity around terms like NCERT.

new_tests.text: GET READY NOW, seats are LIMITED!
Enroll for JEE and NEET with IIT faculty.

results.title: Respectful, inclusive language
results.before: Describe students by what they need, not by labels. Address everyone, not only boys.

dismissals.text: We never call anyone weak students. Every student gets a mentor.
Hey guys, a parent asked us not to write this, so from now on it is hi everyone.

proposal.description: Do not refer to learners with ability-based labels or gendered slang; use neutral, need-focused language that treats all students equally.
proposal.pass_example: Extra classes for students who need more support.
proposal.what_changed: Clarified that any ability-based label (e.g., "weak") and any gendered colloquial address (e.g., "guys") are prohibited, so the boundary is unmistakable.

new_tests.text: Extra classes for students who need more support.

results.title: No false urgency
results.before: Do not pressure the reader with scarcity or countdowns. State the real date or the real number of seats instead.

dismissals.text: No need to hurry: admissions stay open until 31 March.
This is not your last chance. You can join the batch in any month.

proposal.description: Do not create artificial urgency; only mention a deadline, start date, seat count, or other time-limited fact that is true and verifiable for this offering.
proposal.pass_example: The next batch starts on 1 December and has 20 seats available.
proposal.what_changed: Clarified that the rule bans any fabricated scarcity or countdown language, not just the words 'hurry' or 'last chance', by tying the prohibition to false, unverified urgency claims.

new_tests.text: The next batch starts on 1 December and has 20 seats available.

results.title: Confident, never hype
results.before: PrepPath sounds calm and sure of itself. No shouting, no stacked exclamation marks, no words in capitals for emphasis.

dismissals.text: Happy Diwali!! Classes resume on 4 November.
Congratulations, Diya!! Your mentor is proud of you.

proposal.description: Do not use multiple consecutive exclamation marks, all-caps words, or ALL-CAPS for emphasis; a single exclamation mark is allowed only in a friendly, informal greeting.
proposal.pass_example: Results are out. We're proud of every student.
proposal.what_changed: Clarified that any run of two or more exclamation marks and any all-caps word are prohibited, while a single exclamation is permitted only in a greeting, eliminating the previous vague "no shouting" wording.

new_tests.text: Results are out. We're proud of every student.

proposal.description: Any copy that states a specific selection count, rank, score, or result for a test, exam, or program must include the approved disclaimer D-1 in the same language as the claim.
proposal.flag_example: Our students achieved a 95% pass rate in the 2024 JEE exam.
proposal.pass_example: Our students achieved a 95% pass rate in the 2024 JEE exam. Disclaimer D-1: Past results do not guarantee future performance.
proposal.what_changed: Clarified that the rule covers any explicit mention of selections, ranks, scores, or results—not just aggregated numbers—so reviewers can see that statements about batch ranks also require the disclaimer.

proposal.description: Only use superlative or ranking words such as "#1", "best", "top", "leading", etc. when an approved, verifiable fact in the register directly supports the specific claim.
proposal.flag_example: Our coaching is the best in India.
proposal.pass_example: Our coaching is highly regarded, with a 95% pass rate among students.
proposal.what_changed: Added "leading" to the list of prohibited superlatives and clarified that any ranking word requires a registered, verifiable fact, fixing the ambiguity that caused "best coaching" and "leading coaching" to be inconsistently flagged.
